Thank you for choosing to send your work entitled "Capturing the Temporal Evolution of Choice in Prefrontal Cortex" for consideration at eLife. Your full submission has been evaluated by Eve Marder (Senior editor), Michael Frank (Reviewing editor), and two peer reviewers, and the decision was reached after discussions between the reviewers. Based on our discussions and the individual reviews below, we regret to inform you that your work will not be considered further for publication in eLife in its current form.

We should note first that all involved expressed interest in the findings and the high quality work, but questioned the significance and insight afforded by the work over and above what your group has published in the Nature Neuroscience article, which showed how the time course of various value-related signals are replicated using the attractor models. The main issues that came up in the review discussion (some of which are reiterated by the individual reviewer comments below) are as follows. First, both reviewers thought that the conclusions were overstated. They felt that while the PCA analysis was interesting, just because some of the variance in chosen value signals could be accounted for by a latency-based PC, that does not itself make the chosen value signal functionally irrelevant (epiphenomenal) (and even then, some variance remained). They also weren't compelled by the implication that the signals are pre-decisional rather than post-decisional, given that it is very difficult to infer when a decision was made (i.e. to show that the signal emerges when LFP is still ramping does not necessarily imply that it was prior to the decision). It was felt that it is equally plausible and perhaps more likely that CV signals are emerging as decisions are formed, and that CV signals have multiple functions, depending on the time point.

That said, we agree that the single-trial metric of LFP ERP latency does seem like a nice innovation. And its relationship to task variables (chosen value and error commission) provides some validation. But the reviewers were equally concerned about the relationship with effort vs delay signals given the timing of the observed variables, and the significance of the LFP latency metric's relationship to spiking activity seems murkier.

Thus we are rejecting the paper on the grounds that the main new analyses are not as compelling as would be needed for eLife. If you feel strongly that you can address these criticisms with new analyses and reframe the paper so that it is in-line with what can be concluded from the data given the concerns, we could consider a new submission, but again the new insights afforded beyond your previous work (beside the discovery of a PC component that relates to ERP latency) would have to be quite clear.

Reviewer #1:

This manuscript by Hunt et al. is based on the analyses of several different types of data collected from multiple experiments that have been described in previous papers. The most important piece of data was the single-neuron activity recorded from 3 different cortical areas, including the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), and orbitofrontal cortex (OFC). The authors have also analyzed the local field potential (LFP) data collected from these areas in the same experiment. The results obtained from these analyses were then compared to the results from the human MEG experiment and their network model, which is based on an influential model of Wang (2002). Through a set of clever analyses, the authors draw their main conclusion that a trial-by-trial index of decision dynamics, derived from the PCA analysis of LFP data, was largely correlated with the chosen value. Most interestingly, this index was used to demonstrate that the functional interactions between different cortical areas reflect the type of information considered during decision making (e.g., delay vs. effort). However, there are several major weaknesses in this manuscript.

1) The authors argue that the chosen value signals are epiphenomenon based on the fact that the chosen value signals encoded by individual neurons can be substantially diminished by the PCA-based trial-by-trial index of the decision process measured from the local activity. This argument is not convincing. It appears that the same logic, if applied to other types of signals encoded by any neurons, would make virtually any kind of neural signals epiphenomenon. In other words, the fact that a certain type of signal encoded by a given neuron can be accounted for by the local dynamics of its surrounding network does not mean that the encoded signal has no functional significance.

2) Although the dynamic changes in the functional connectivity identified by this analysis related to effort vs. delay condition are interesting, the time course of this difference is not consistent with the authors' conclusion. The results shown in Figure 5 indicate that the difference does not arise until 600 ms after the onset of the choice period. However, the chosen action signals in the DLPFC begin to emerge within 200 ms from the onset of the choice period, and reach its first asymptotic level before 400 ms. Therefore, the communication between DLPFC and ACC/OFC identified in this analysis is unlikely to be the main driver for the choice signals in the DLPFC.

3) It is not clear whether the use of PCA (i.e., PC2) is really necessary to derive the main conclusion of this study, because an alternative possibility is that the explanatory power of PC2 might be largely due to the similarity of its temporal profile with that of chosen value signals (shown in Figure 1B). If this is the case, then the fact that PC2 is correlated with the chosen value signal (Figure 2E) is not too surprising.

Reviewer #2:

This paper reports a monkey electrophysiology study of two-alternative value-based decision making, focusing on the temporal evolution of decision-related neural signals in DLPFC, ACC, and OFC. Main findings include the following:

a) DLPFC spiking activity appeared to progress from a graded encoding of the relative action values to a discrete encoding of the selected action.

b) LFPs in all 3 regions positively encoded the chosen option's value throughout the choice epoch, but shifted from a positive-signed to a negative-signed encoding of the unchosen option's value. This can be interpreted as a progression from encoding "value sum" to "value difference".

c) Single-trial LFPs were summarized using two PCA-based indices that reflected the overall amplitude and latency of the waveform, respectively. These indices scaled with the value of the chosen option, and also showed an association with spiking activity.

d) DLPFC spiking was associated with LFP latency in other regions. The association was stronger with OFC when delay-related costs were at stake, and stronger with ACC when effort-related costs were at stake.

Parallel analyses were applied both to a human MEG data set and to the behaviour of a neural network model, and some of the same effects were obtained. The application of directly parallel analyses to multiple modalities of neural data is a significant strength of the paper. The development of trial-wise indices of LFP latency is likewise a potentially important contribution.

Comments:

1) The paper has a very cogent Introduction pointing out the challenge of reading out static decision variables from dynamic processes. But some of the rhetoric around this topic seems to go beyond what the data support. The authors express skepticism that neural activity represents economic variables (the word "represent" frequently appears in scare-quotes). But the idea that neural signals evolve dynamically isn't incompatible with the idea that they represent economic variables. This paper's conclusions really seem to pertain to how, rather than whether, economic variables are neurally represented. The results suggest that chosen value, for example, is encoded in the LFP amplitude in a specific time window (e.g. around 400 ms where PC2 peaks, indicative of the latency of the underlying waveform), rather than, say, the overall peak of the evoked LFP.

2) Trial-by-trial LFP-derived indices are shown to be related to spiking activity, but it's not entirely clear how to relate this finding to what is already known about spike/LFP coupling. Could this effect be accounted for in terms of straightforward first-order correlations between the spiking and LFP time courses? What makes this seem plausible is that the time course of PC2 weights (Figure 2B) looks similar to the time course of PC2 effects on spiking (Figure 3). Spikes and LFPs were recorded from different electrodes to avoid contamination, but it's still possible that a genuine relationship holds between the two (to mention just one previous example, a general negative correlation between multi-unit activity and LFP is shown in Whittingstall & Logothetis, 2009, Figure 1A).

3) I don't follow the logic of the analysis in the subsection “Chosen value correlates as an epiphenomenon of varying decision dynamics”. In a regression model of spike rates, predictors for LFP-derived PC1 and PC2 steal variance away from a "chosen value" predictor but not from other task-related predictors. This is taken to imply that "chosen value" effects are mainly picking up on the latency of the neural response. But this result actually seems consistent with these effects being related to either amplitude (PC1) or latency (PC2). The latency interpretation would be on stronger footing if it could be shown that chosen value effects varied with the addition/removal of PC2 only.

4) I'm concerned about whether it's appropriate to treat LFPs from simultaneously recorded electrodes as independent observations. Panel A of Figure 4—figure supplement 2 shows that LFP features are highly correlated across electrodes, even in different brain regions. This probably isn't a problem for the PCA decomposition, but it does seem like an issue for inferential tests of associations between LFP and task variables. For example, Figure 1D and 1E plot "mean /- s.e. across electrodes"-but since multiple electrodes were recorded per trial, the nominal number of electrodes may be larger than the true number of independent observations. The same concern applies to the results in Figure 2E and related figures. It would be helpful for the paper to clarify how interdependence among electrodes was dealt with.

[Editors’ note: what now follows is the decision letter after the authors submitted for further consideration.]

Thank you for resubmitting your work entitled "Capturing the temporal evolution of choice in prefrontal cortex" for further consideration at eLife. Your revised article has been favorably evaluated by Eve Marder (Senior editor), Michael Frank (Reviewing editor), and three reviewers, including a new referee who was not involved in the previous round of review. They all agree that the manuscript has been improved and the novel contributions are clear and worthwhile relative to the previous work. However, there are some remaining issues that need to be addressed, as outlined below.

1) The authors claim that the PC2 from LFP provides a measure of local dynamics that is more specific (and relevant to unit activity) than larger scale global dynamics. The analysis provided by the authors (effect of local LFP after orthogonalizing on LFP from another region) is encouraging in this regard, however supporting the claim would also require showing that the opposite is not true (i.e. that running the analysis in reverse does not yield the same result). The correlation coefficients in the histograms of Figure 4—figure supplement 3 suggest that this may be the case, although there does not seem to be much of a within region advantage for DLPFC in particular. Also, as far as I can tell, the authors did not incorporate reaction time, which is typically used as a trial-by-trial indicator of decision dynamics, into these analyses. I suspect that this is because the required delay is sufficiently long to create a floor effect on RTs, however if this is the case it deserves mention in the text. Otherwise the authors should test whether LFP measures relate to the "chosen value" aspects of neural activity after accounting for RT.

2) The authors show that PC2 captures variance in neural firing that is typically ascribed to chosen value. I agree with the authors that this is an important point. Yet I found the interpretation of this point to be somewhat overly specific: "We therefore questioned whether chosen value coding might simply be a consequence of the same neural dynamics occurring at varying latencies across trials." This is certainly one interpretation of the authors' results, but not the only one. Another (more standard) interpretation of this finding is that the LFP components mediate the chosen value representations at the level of single units. Given that the LFPs are often interpreted as measurements of local synaptic input, I find this interpretation to be fairly reasonable and consistent with the data provided. The finding that PC1 (which does not contain timing information) also steals variance from chosen value may even provide some specific evidence for this interpretation. As I understand it, the main reason that the authors' interpret the data in terms of dynamics is provided in the final analysis showing that in an attractor network of decision-making the same sorts of signals emerge as a byproduct of competition. I think in order to improve the clarity it would be useful to avoid specific interpretations of causality until the Discussion section where both possibilities should be discussed.

3) Relatedly, another reviewer noted that the most direct evidence for the notion that chosen-value effects emerge from "the same choice dynamics occurring at different rates on different trials" is derived from the analysis on p. 10, but I'm afraid I'm still not onboard with the logic of this. The authors foreground an analysis showing that the chosen-value effect in spike rates is reduced by jointly including PC1 (indexing LFP amplitude) and PC2 (indexing LFP latency) in the regression model (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, and Figure 4—figure supplement 3). I still don't see how this is germane to their conclusion about latency. The specific effect of the latency-related PC2 is now shown as a supplement, and is considerably weaker albeit nonzero. The original chosen-value effect, which peaked at a% CPD of around 0.9 (Figure 1B), is reduced by up to about 0.1 by both PCs together (Figure 4), or 0.03 by PC2 alone (Figure 4—figure supplement 2). So wouldn't it be at least as accurate to conclude that chosen-value effects emerge from the same neural dynamics occurring at different amplitudes across trials? (The predictions of the attractor network are also unclear in this regard, i.e. in the predictions for combination of PCs, and so it seems important that the authors clarify the predictions of the attractor model.) The same concern applies to the local-versus-distal result in Figure 4—figure supplement 3, which is interpreted solely in terms of neural latency but results for PC2 alone are not shown.

It seems to me an easier conclusion to square with the data would be that chosen-value effects originate from a combination of the amplitude and speed of the dynamically unfolding neural response. This may not be so starkly different from existing perspectives, although it's of course still valuable to see the details of how it plays out. The authors could also easily reframe the result that LFP measures partially mediate the chosen value effect and tone down the oppositional framing of decision dynamics versus static chosen value representation. They could use the network model results as a podium to say that chosen value representations need not emerge for the purpose of encoding chosen value, which would be entirely accurate from my standpoint.

4) A similar issue comes up in the section on neural network modeling, which shows that chosen-value effects in the simulation can be explained away by a principal component capturing variability in neural dynamics, but doesn't state clearly enough that "dynamics" here refers, not just to latency, but to a mixture of amplitude and latency (Figure 7—figure supplement 1, panel C). (Related to this, a sentence the sentence “we obtained principal components that controlled waveform amplitude and latency, as in the ERPs" seems inaccurate, since what was actually extracted was a single component that mixed amplitude and latency, unlike the earlier analysis.)

5) The authors use the first principal component of the attractor network model decomposition rather than PC2. While I agree with the authors that this component seems to contain some temporal information, it does seem to mainly capture amplitude. Given that the authors interpret PC2 as if it were the derivative of the ERP, it seems that it would be a bit easier to make the connection between computational model and biology if model signals were decomposed using separate components to capture overall amplitude and derivative. This could be done simply by creating weight vectors based on the average model response (ERP) and the derivative of that signal.

6) The authors note that PC1 relates primarily to value sum, however this does not seem to be the case in ACC, where PC1 takes positive coefficients for chosen value and negative coefficients for unchosen value. This makes me wonder whether the added contributions of PC1 in explaining single unit chosen value effects relate primarily to the inclusion of PC1 from ACC electrodes. In my opinion, such a finding would not necessarily detract from the dynamics idea, as overall ACC signal amplitude may play a role in adjusting decision threshold, which directly affects dynamics. Either way, the authors should make the heterogeneity across recording locations clear in this regard.

7) The section on inter-region correlations (“OFC and ACC dynamics have distinct influences on delay- and effort-based decisions respectively”) is quite specific about causal directionality, concluding that DLPFC activity is influenced by OFC and ACC. It isn't apparent to me that there's any support for this. (A third-variable explanation would be a plausible alternative.)

claims.claim: The brain can use neural representations of decision variables to guide selection of the most valuable alternative.
claims.source: By forming neural representations of such quantities, it is argued that the brain can use these representations to guide selection of the most valuable alternative.
claims.evidence: This describes a theoretical framework in neuroeconomics.

claims.source: Our present understanding of economic decision formation has been founded upon careful study of neural representations of value and how they differ across PFC subregions (Glimcher and Fehr, 2014; Rushworth et al., 2012; Rangel and Hare, 2010).
claims.evidence: This statement summarizes the current state of the field with citations.

claims.claim: An alternative perspective on the origins of neural representations during decision making stems from choice models from mathematical psychology (Busemeyer and Townsend, 1993).

claims.claim: Mathematical psychology models seek to explain decisions in terms of their temporal evolution or dynamics.
claims.source: Such models seek to explain decisions in terms of their temporal evolution or dynamics.
claims.evidence: This describes the key feature of mathematical psychology models.

claims.claim: Mathematical psychology models originally accounted for temporally varying features of behaviour, such as reaction times and eye gaze (Busemeyer and Townsend, 1993; Ratcliff and Rouder, 1998; Krajbich et al., 2010).

claims.claim: Mathematical psychology models have successfully captured temporally varying features of neural activity in the lateral intraparietal cortex (LIP) during perceptual choice (Shadlen and Newsome, 2001; Gold and Shadlen, 2007).

claims.claim: Psychological models can be related to nonlinear attractor network models firmly rooted in neurobiology (Wang, 2002).
claims.source: These psychological models can also be related to other dynamical models (Bogacz et al., 2006) such as nonlinear attractor network models firmly rooted in neurobiology (Wang, 2002).
claims.evidence: This statement connects different modeling approaches with citations.

claims.claim: The common feature of both psychological and neurobiological accounts is that they focus on the temporal evolution of a decision signal across time.
claims.source: The common feature of both psychological and neurobiological accounts is that they focus on the temporal evolution of a decision signal across time, rather than the strength with which it represents decision variables at a particular fixed point in time.
claims.evidence: This statement identifies a key commonality between different modeling approaches.

claims.claim: Even if neuronal activity underwent the exact same physiological process on different trials (such as a ramp-to-threshold), it might nevertheless appear to represent certain economic features of a decision.
claims.source: Contrasting the two perspectives, it becomes apparent that even if neuronal activity underwent the exact same physiological process on different trials (such as a ramp-to-threshold), it might nevertheless appear to represent certain economic features of a decision.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical argument made by the authors to motivate their study.

claims.claim: As the decision unfolds, neural activity will be higher on trials that ramp quickly than on those that ramp slowly.
claims.source: Put simply, as the decision unfolds, neural activity will be higher on trials that ramp quickly than on those that ramp slowly.
claims.evidence: This is a logical consequence of the ramp-to-threshold model.

claims.claim: Neural activity will correlate with any variable that affects the decision speed.
claims.source: It will therefore correlate with any variable that affects the decision speed, and this effect will appear most prominent at timepoints in the trial when the ramping process, or rate of change, is maximal.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the dynamics of decision-making.

claims.claim: Economic variables that predict the rate of change would appear to be represented in neural activity if analysed without knowledge of the underlying dynamics.
claims.source: Even in more complex dynamical situations, it is easy to see how economic variables that predict the rate of change would appear to be represented in neural activity if analysed without knowledge of the underlying dynamics.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical argument about how analysis methods can affect interpretation.

claims.claim: The value of the chosen item ('chosen value') strongly affects behavioural reaction times in economic choice tasks.
claims.source: This might particularly be true of the value of the chosen item ('chosen value'), which strongly affects behavioural reaction times in economic choice tasks.
claims.evidence: This statement describes a known relationship between chosen value and reaction time.

claims.claim: The neuroeconomic perspective often labels chosen value representations as a 'post-decision' signal.
claims.source: The neuroeconomic perspective often labels chosen value representations as a 'post-decision' signal, arguing that chosen value signals do not reflect the decision competition itself but instead the outcome of the comparison process (Cai and Padoa-Schioppa, 2012; Blanchard and Hayden, 2014).
claims.evidence: This describes a common interpretation in the neuroeconomics literature with citations.

claims.claim: One interpretation of chosen value representations is that they are needed for subsequent computation of a reward prediction error (Rangel and Hare, 2010).
claims.source: One interpretation of such representations is that they are needed for subsequent computation of a reward prediction error (Rangel and Hare, 2010).
claims.evidence: This describes a functional interpretation of chosen value signals with a citation.

claims.claim: The dynamical perspective proposes that chosen value representations may originate as a consequence of time evolving decision processes.
claims.source: Yet the dynamical perspective proposes that they may in fact originate as a consequence of time evolving decision processes.
claims.evidence: This presents an alternative interpretation that the authors explore in their study.

claims.claim: The dynamical perspective argues that chosen value correlates inevitably emerge as a decision is made.
claims.source: Rather than casting a chosen value representation as signaling 'pre-decision' or 'post-decision' variables to downstream brain areas, it argues that such correlates inevitably emerge as a decision is made.
claims.evidence: This describes a key theoretical claim of the dynamical perspective.

claims.claim: In its most extreme form, the dynamical hypothesis might contend that chosen value signals would be fully accounted for by variation in underlying decision rates.
claims.source: In its most extreme form, this hypothesis might contend that chosen value signals would be fully accounted for by variation in underlying decision rates.
claims.evidence: This presents a strong version of the hypothesis that the authors test.

claims.claim: It is critical to index how neural dynamics unfold on individual trials to assess the dynamical hypothesis.
claims.source: To assess this proposal more carefully, it becomes critical to index how neural dynamics unfold on individual trials.
claims.evidence: This identifies a methodological requirement for testing the hypothesis.

claims.claim: Tackling the problem of indexing neural dynamics in PFC provides unique challenges.
claims.source: In PFC, tackling this problem provides unique challenges.
claims.evidence: This statement identifies PFC as particularly challenging for studying dynamics.

claims.claim: Several recent studies have recovered single-trial dynamical information in structures close to motor output, based upon neuronal spiking data (Thura and Cisek, 2014; Kaufman et al., 2015; Murakami et al., 2014; Bollimunta et al., 2012; Kiani et al., 2014; Carnevale et al., 2015).
claims.source: Several recent studies have recovered single-trial dynamical information in structures close to motor output, based upon neuronal spiking data (Thura and Cisek, 2014; Kaufman et al., 2015; Murakami et al., 2014; Bollimunta et al., 2012; Kiani et al., 2014; Carnevale et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This statement reviews recent methodological advances with citations.

claims.claim: The distance of PFC from either sensory input or motor output produces neural activity that is poorly aligned with simple features of the experimental task (Rigotti et al., 2013).
claims.source: Yet the distance of PFC from either sensory input or motor output produces neural activity that is poorly aligned with simple features of the experimental task (Rigotti et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This statement describes a characteristic of PFC activity with a citation.

claims.claim: Attempts to understand PFC activity should extract its dynamical state based on neural information alone.
claims.source: Attempts to understand PFC activity should therefore extract its dynamical state based on neural information alone, rather than first sorting spike trains by motor output or experimental variables as is common in other approaches.
claims.evidence: This is a methodological recommendation made by the authors.

claims.claim: It is unclear whether neuronal firing rates are the most reliable source of single-trial information.
claims.source: It is also unclear whether neuronal firing rates are in fact the most reliable source of single-trial information.
claims.evidence: This statement questions a common assumption in the field.

claims.claim: The esotericism of PFC neuronal responses is compounded by a high degree of stochasticity in neuronal spike trains, delivering statistical challenges to obtaining single-trial information (Churchland et al., 2007; Park et al., 2014).
claims.source: The esotericism of PFC neuronal responses is compounded by a high degree of stochasticity in neuronal spike trains, delivering statistical challenges to obtaining single-trial information (Churchland et al., 2007; Park et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This statement describes a technical challenge with citations.

claims.claim: Current techniques sometimes overcome the stochasticity problem by examining tens or hundreds of simultaneously recorded single neurons (Churchland et al., 2007).

claims.evidence: This describes a current methodological approach with a citation.

claims.claim: Data from tens or hundreds of simultaneously recorded neurons is rarely available in humans.
claims.source: Whilst this can be fruitful, such data is rarely available in humans, where the contribution of PFC to value-guided choice is most critical.
claims.evidence: This statement identifies a limitation of current methods for human studies.

claims.claim: The authors sought an alternative index of single-trial neural dynamics that overcame the limitations of spike-based approaches.
claims.source: In the present study, we therefore sought an alternative index of single-trial neural dynamics that overcame these limitations.
claims.evidence: This describes the motivation for the methodological approach taken in the study.

claims.claim: The authors focussed on observations at the mesoscopic scale of the local field potential (LFP).
claims.source: We focussed on observations at the mesoscopic scale of the local field potential (LFP).

claims.claim: LFP can be easily related to simultaneously recorded neuronal spike trains on a trial-by-trial basis in animals.
claims.source: One advantage of this approach is that it can be easily related to simultaneously recorded neuronal spike trains on a trial-by-trial basis in animals

claims.claim: LFP underlies the magnetoencephalography (MEG) signal observable in humans (Buzsáki et al., 2012).
claims.source: but also underlies the magnetoencephalography (MEG) signal observable in humans (Buzsáki et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This statement connects LFP to MEG with a citation.

claims.claim: The authors could recover dynamical information from electrophysiology recordings in macaque monkeys and from non-invasive magnetoencephalography (MEG) recordings in humans.
claims.source: As such, we could recover dynamical information from electrophysiology recordings in macaque monkeys and also from non-invasive magnetoencephalography (MEG) recordings in humans.
claims.evidence: This describes the application of the method to both species.

claims.claim: The LFP-based index provides an important bridge between observations at microscopic (cellular) and macroscopic (whole-brain) scales.
claims.source: This provides an important bridge between observations at microscopic (cellular) and macroscopic (whole-brain) scales.
claims.evidence: This describes a key advantage of the approach.

claims.claim: The index provides information about the speed of a local internal neural decision process that goes beyond a simple behavioural measure of reaction time.
claims.source: Importantly, our index provides information about the speed of a local internal neural decision process that goes beyond a simple behavioural measure of reaction time.
claims.evidence: This describes a key feature of the index developed in the study.

claims.claim: There is a temporal evolution from action value difference to chosen action signals that are selectively present in dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) neurons, but not anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) or orbitofrontal cortex (OFC).
claims.source: We first demonstrate a temporal evolution from action value difference to chosen action signals that are selectively present in dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) neurons, but not anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) or orbitofrontal cortex (OFC).

claims.claim: Correlates of 'chosen value' are ubiquitously encoded across DLPFC, ACC, and OFC.
claims.source: This contrasts against the ubiquitous encoding across all three subregions of 'chosen value'.

claims.claim: Correlates of chosen value may arise as a consequence of dynamical processing, as opposed to being purely represented as a neuroeconomic post-decision variable.

claims.claim: Functional interactions between PFC subregions can be reshaped in a task-dependent manner.
claims.source: Next, by simultaneously indexing decision formation across multiple PFC subregions, we show that functional interactions can be reshaped in a task-dependent manner.

claims.claim: OFC and ACC dynamics selectively influence dorsolateral DLPFC activity on delay- and effort-based decisions respectively.
claims.source: We find that OFC and ACC dynamics selectively influence dorsolateral DLPFC activity on delay- and effort-based decisions respectively.
claims.evidence: This is a key finding stated in the introduction and demonstrated in Figure 5.

claims.claim: The observations can be related to predictions from a dynamical neural network model of choice.
claims.source: Finally, our observations can be related to predictions from a dynamical neural network model of choice.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction and demonstrated in Figure 7.

claims.claim: The study provides formal links to established dynamical mechanisms underlying perceptual decision-making.
claims.source: This provides formal links to established dynamical mechanisms underlying perceptual decision-making.
claims.evidence: This describes a theoretical contribution of the study.

claims.claim: Single neuron firing and local field potentials (LFPs) were recorded simultaneously from three PFC subregions in four macaque monkeys: orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC).
claims.source: We examined a study of cost-benefit decision making in which single neuron firing and local field potentials (LFPs) were recorded simultaneously from three PFC subregions fundamental to value-guided choice in four macaque monkeys: orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental setup of the study.

claims.claim: On each trial, subjects chose between two pictures that led to a certain reward magnitude (quantity of fruit juice) after paying a certain cost.
claims.source: On each trial, subjects chose between two pictures that led to a certain reward magnitude (quantity of fruit juice) after paying a certain cost (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental task shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: On half of trials the cost was physical effort needed to obtain reward, and on half of trials it was delay to reward.
claims.source: On half of trials this cost was physical effort needed to obtain reward, and on half of trials it was delay to reward.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claims.claim: Subjects were overtrained on the cost and benefit paired with each picture.
claims.source: Subjects were overtrained on the cost and benefit paired with each picture.
claims.evidence: This describes the training procedure.

claims.claim: Subjects' choices were well described by a linear trade-off between reward and cost combined with a softmax choice function.
claims.source: Their choices were well described by a linear trade-off between reward and cost combined with a softmax choice function (see Hosokawa et al., 2013 for detailed behavioural modelling).
claims.evidence: This describes the behavioral modeling results with a citation.

claims.claim: Neural activity was analyzed during a 1s choice phase, when subjects fixated centrally whilst both pictures were on screen.
claims.source: Throughout the paper, we analyse neuronal firing and LFP during a 1s choice phase, when subjects fixated centrally whilst both pictures were on screen.
claims.evidence: This describes the analysis window for the study.

claims.claim: After the 1s choice phase, a go cue appeared, instructing subjects to saccade to their preferred picture to indicate their choice.
claims.source: After this 1s period, a go cue appeared, instructing subjects to saccade to their preferred picture to indicate their choice.
claims.evidence: This describes the task structure.

claims.claim: Early in the trial, value correlates in DLPFC were found in the reference frame of action value difference (i.e. left minus right saccade value influenced neural firing).
claims.source: Early in the trial, value correlates were found in the reference frame of action value difference (i.e. left minus right saccade value influenced neural firing; Figure 1B, blue)

claims.claim: DLPFC neurons that showed strong selectivity for left minus right saccade option value 300 ms after decision onset also showed strong selectivity for left minus right choices 700 ms after decision onset.
claims.source: DLPFC neurons that showed strong selectivity for left minus right saccade option value 300 ms after decision onset also showed strong selectivity for left minus right choices 700 ms after decision onset (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: The temporal evolution from action value difference to categorical choice was selectively present in DLPFC, but not ACC or OFC.
claims.source: This temporal evolution from action value difference to categorical choice was selectively present in DLPFC, but not ACC (n = 321 neurons) or OFC (n = 212 neurons) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: All three regions (DLPFC, ACC, OFC) showed correlates of chosen value with a similar timecourse.
claims.source: Notably, however, all three regions showed correlates of chosen value with a similar timecourse (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the text and shown in the figures.

claims.claim: The overall shape of the choice phase evoked LFP was surprisingly consistent across PFC subregions.
claims.source: The overall shape of the choice phase evoked LFP was surprisingly consistent across PFC subregions (Figure 1D) and subjects (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in the figures.

claims.claim: All PFC areas contained a fast biphasic component shortly after sensory input, and a slower component lasting several hundred milliseconds after this.
claims.source: All areas contained a fast biphasic component shortly after sensory input, and a slower component lasting several hundred milliseconds after this.
claims.evidence: This describes features of the evoked LFP response visible in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: Early in the trial (~250 ms) value correlates in LFP were positive for both chosen and unchosen value.
claims.source: Early in the trial (~250 ms) value correlates were positive for both chosen and unchosen value
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: Later in the trial (~450 ms) value correlates for unchosen value flipped to become negatively signed.
claims.source: but later in the trial (~450 ms) value correlates for unchosen value flipped to become negatively signed.
claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: LFP value correlates show a temporal evolution from an early representation of value sum (=chosen+unchosen value) to a later representation of value difference (=chosen-unchosen value).
claims.source: This implies a temporal evolution from an early representation of value sum (=chosen+unchosen value) to a later representation of value difference (=chosen-unchosen value).
claims.evidence: This interpretation is stated in the text based on the pattern shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: The progression of LFP value correlates is notably similar to observations made in human PFC during value-guided choice using MEG (Hunt et al., 2012).
claims.source: This progression is notably similar to observations made in human PFC during value-guided choice using MEG (Hunt et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This statement connects the current findings to previous work with a citation.

claims.claim: LFP value correlates were maximal when the event-related LFP was ramping, not peaking.
claims.source: Crucially, these value correlates were maximal when the event-related LFP was ramping, not peaking (that is, when the temporal derivative of the LFP was large [Figure 1F]).
claims.evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: Chosen and unchosen value influence the rate at which LFP dynamics unfold on each trial, rather than being explicitly represented by the amplitude of an evoked response.
claims.source: This suggests chosen and unchosen value influence the rate at which LFP dynamics unfold on each trial, rather than being explicitly represented by the amplitude of an evoked response.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the data pattern shown in Figures 1E and 1F.

claims.claim: The evoked LFP appeared consistent across different recording electrodes and sessions.

claims.evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The evoked LFP possessed a high single-trial signal to noise ratio.
claims.source: and possessed a high single-trial signal to noise ratio (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.source: For each subject, the input data for macaque PCA was decision-locked raw LFP data, stacked across all electrodes from all recording sessions to form a large matrix X.
claims.evidence: This describes the data preparation for PCA analysis.

claims.source: PCA decomposes X into temporal principal components V, with dimensions nTimepoints by nComponents, and component weights U, with dimensions nSingleTrials by nComponents (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This describes the output of the PCA decomposition shown in Figure 2A.

claims.source: The principal components (PCs) in V provide a set of temporal basis functions (Figure 2B) that capture the principal modes of variation in the shape of the waveform across trials.
claims.evidence: This describes the interpretation of the principal components shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The single-trial weights in U tell us how much of each PC is present in each single-trial response.

claims.evidence: This describes the interpretation of the PC weights.

claims.claim: The decomposition has the same meaning across different electrodes and recording sessions because data are stacked.
claims.source: Because data are stacked, however, the decomposition has the same meaning across different electrodes and recording sessions.
claims.evidence: This explains an advantage of the stacking approach.

claims.claim: The first and second principal components were strikingly consistent across all four macaque subjects.

claims.claim: PC1 resembled the basic shape of the event-related field potential.

claims.claim: Adding or subtracting PC1 captures variation across trials in response amplitude.

claims.claim: Adding or subtracting the temporal derivative of a waveform controls the latency at which it peaks (Friston et al., 1998; Mayhew et al., 2006).
claims.source: Adding or subtracting the temporal derivative of a waveform controls the latency at which it peaks (Figure 2D, right panel) (Friston et al., 1998; Mayhew et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is a known property of temporal derivatives cited from the literature and illustrated in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Knowledge about PC2 weights provides a parsimonious description of single-trial ERP latencies.
claims.source: Knowledge about PC2 weights therefore provides a parsimonious description of single-trial ERP latencies, a key feature of the dynamical ERP response.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the meaning of PC2 weights.

claims.claim: PC2 weights correlate with the phase of low frequency (theta frequency [4-8 Hz]) oscillations during the decision period.

claims.evidence: This finding is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Factors modulating reaction time in value-based choice studies would affect the weight of PC2, controlling the latency of the LFP waveform.

claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis stated by the authors based on their interpretation of PC2.

claims.claim: Chosen value had a strong and consistent effect on PC2 across all regions studied.

claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of PC2 weights based on the data and cited literature.

claims.evidence: This is stated as a result of additional control analyses.

results.result: A single-trial index of PFC internal states was recovered using PCA decomposition of LFP data from macaque monkeys and MEG data from humans. PC1 captured waveform amplitude while PC2 captured waveform latency, with PC2 weights providing a neurally-derived index of decision speed on each trial that was influenced by chosen value and error trials.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C95 describe a well-validated methodological approach using PCA to extract single-trial dynamics from LFP/MEG data. The consistency of PC1 and PC2 across subjects (C83), their interpretable effects on waveform properties (C84-C88), and their relationship to decision variables (C91-C94) provide converging evidence. The method is applied to both macaque and human data (C45, C117-C121), demonstrating cross-species validity.

results.result: DLPFC neurons show a temporal evolution from encoding action value difference early in the trial to encoding chosen action late in the trial. This temporal evolution was selectively present in DLPFC but not in ACC or OFC.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C65 provide consistent evidence from single-unit recordings showing the temporal dynamics of value coding in DLPFC (n=303 neurons). The finding is strengthened by the correlation between early action value selectivity and late choice selectivity (C64) and the regional specificity demonstrated by comparison with ACC and OFC (C65).

results.result: Correlates of chosen value were ubiquitously encoded across DLPFC, ACC, and OFC with similar timecourses.
results.evaluation: Claims C49 and C66 are directly supported by data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, demonstrating that all three PFC subregions encode chosen value with similar temporal profiles, contrasting with the region-specific encoding of action value difference and chosen action.

results.result: Correlates of chosen value in single neurons may arise as a consequence of dynamical processing. Including LFP-derived PC1/PC2 as coregressors caused a significant reduction in chosen value coding but not in action value difference or chosen action coding, suggesting that some variance attributed to chosen value originates from local dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C100 and C150 present a key finding supported by regression analyses (Figure 4). The authors appropriately acknowledge caveats (C151-C153) including that only partial variance was explained and that observation noise may limit the estimates. The finding is further validated by control analyses using noise components and by showing greater reduction with local vs. distal PC weights (C100).

results.result: Functional interactions between PFC subregions can be reshaped in a task-dependent manner. OFC dynamics selectively influence DLPFC activity on delay-based trials while ACC dynamics selectively influence DLPFC activity on effort-based trials.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C112 describe a well-controlled analysis showing task-specific influences of ACC and OFC on DLPFC firing (n=124 DLPFC units with simultaneous recordings). The finding is strengthened by control analyses showing the effect was not present in reverse directions (C107) and by the temporal specificity of the effects (C108-C112). The result extends prior lesion and imaging findings (C101, C159-C161) cited in C162.

results.result: DLPFC neurons with high chosen value selectivity were preferentially influenced by other regions' dynamics in a task-dependent manner, while neurons with low chosen value selectivity were not. This effect was specific to chosen value selectivity and not found for response selectivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C115 describe a median split analysis (Figure 5B) showing that the task-dependent inter-regional influences specifically affect neurons encoding chosen value. The control analysis (C115) showing no effect for response-selective neurons strengthens the interpretation that this relates to decision dynamics rather than motor preparation.

results.result: The single-trial index describes the relationship between neural dynamics and behavior in both human and monkey PFC, directly bridging between human MEG data and underlying neuronal activity. Human MEG data showed similar PC1/PC2 relationships to macaque LFP, with PC2 correlating with chosen value, error trials, and reaction times.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C122 demonstrate successful application of the PCA method to human MEG data from ventromedial PFC, showing similar relationships between PC1/PC2 and decision variables as in macaque data. The additional finding that PC2 correlates with reaction times (C121) provides behavioral validation. This cross-species validation is a key strength of the study.

results.result: The observations can be explained mechanistically via a recurrent neural network model of choice. The model reproduced the temporal profile of value correlates in DLPFC neurons and showed that internal dynamics extracted from PCA explained chosen value coding similarly to the data.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C133 describe modeling results using a spiking attractor network (Wang, 2002 parameters). The model successfully reproduced key features of the data including temporal evolution of value correlates (C126) and the reduction in chosen value coding when dynamics are accounted for (C132). The authors note discrepancies (C127-C129) between model and data, demonstrating appropriate critical evaluation.

results.result: The evoked LFP during the choice phase was surprisingly consistent across PFC subregions and subjects, containing a fast biphasic component and a slower component, with high single-trial signal-to-noise ratio.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C68 and C75-C76 describe basic properties of the LFP data shown in Figures 1D, 2—figure supplement 1, and 2—figure supplement 2. These observations provide the foundation for the PCA approach and are well-documented in the figures.

results.result: LFP value correlates showed a temporal evolution from representing value sum early (~250 ms) to value difference later (~450 ms). These correlates were maximal when the LFP was ramping rather than peaking, suggesting that chosen and unchosen value influence the rate at which dynamics unfold.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C74 describe the temporal dynamics of value coding in LFP (Figure 1E-F). The observation that value correlates peak during ramping phases (C73) is a key insight supporting the dynamical interpretation (C74). The similarity to previous human MEG findings (C72) provides cross-validation.

results.result: PC2 weights correlated with the phase of theta frequency (4-8 Hz) oscillations during the decision period.
results.evaluation: Claims C89 and C166 describe a finding shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3. This provides additional validation that PC2 captures latency-related dynamics, as phase shifts in low-frequency oscillations correspond to latency changes. The finding is appropriately presented as supporting evidence rather than a primary result.

results.result: Chosen value had a strong effect on PC2 across all regions, with higher chosen value associated with more positive PC2 (earlier waveform peaks). Error trials also showed more positive PC2 than correct trials. PC1 was primarily influenced by value sum.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C93 and C96 describe regression results shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 5. The effects are statistically significant and consistent across regions (excluding monkey K, analyzed separately in Figure 2—figure supplement 4). These findings validate PC2 as an index of decision speed.

results.result: 44.9% of DLPFC neurons showed significant modulation by LFP-derived PC2 weights during the choice epoch, and this relationship could not be explained by simple first-order correlations between LFP amplitude and firing rate.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C98 provide statistical evidence (p<0.01, corrected for multiple comparisons) that PC2 weights explain variance in single-unit firing beyond what can be attributed to simple LFP-spike correlations. The control analysis (C98) strengthens the interpretation that PC2 captures meaningful dynamics.

results.result: The experimental setup involved simultaneous recordings from OFC, ACC, and DLPFC in four macaque monkeys performing a cost-benefit decision task with effort and delay trials. Subjects were overtrained and their choices were well-described by a linear trade-off model.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C61 describe the experimental methods and task design, which are clearly documented in Figure 1A and the Methods section. The behavioral modeling (C59) is cited to previous work (Hosokawa et al., 2013), appropriately deferring detailed validation to that publication.

results.result: Economic descriptions of PFC activity fail to capture decision dynamics. Indexing neural dynamics in PFC is challenging due to poor alignment with task features, high stochasticity in spike trains, and limited availability of large-scale recordings in humans. The authors sought an alternative LFP-based approach to overcome these limitations.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C3 and C32-C41 articulate the motivation for the study, identifying methodological challenges in the field (supported by citations C34-C39) and justifying the LFP-based approach (C41-C42). This provides appropriate context for the methodological innovation.

results.result: The dynamical perspective proposes that even if neuronal activity underwent the same physiological process (e.g., ramp-to-threshold) on different trials, it might appear to represent economic variables due to trial-by-trial variation in decision speed. Chosen value correlates may emerge as a consequence of time-evolving decision processes.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C31 present the theoretical framework motivating the study. While these are conceptual arguments (INFERENCE/SPECULATION), they are well-reasoned and supported by the empirical findings presented in the paper (particularly C50, C99-C100, C150). The hypothesis is appropriately tested rather than simply asserted.

results.result: The widespread encoding of chosen value has been debated in the literature. The authors argue that what appears as encoding of decision-related signals may be a consequence of dynamical processes. In DLPFC, chosen value correlates occurred maximally during the transformation from action value difference to chosen action, and similar patterns were found in the network model.
results.evaluation: Claims C134-C149 synthesize the discussion of results in the context of prior literature. The conceptual framework is well-supported by the empirical findings (C148-C149 reference Figure 1B and Figure 7B). The authors appropriately acknowledge that chosen value signals may retain functional significance (C145) while proposing a new perspective on their generation.

results.result: The authors note caveats that chosen value correlates may be explained by different mechanisms at different points in the trial, and that correlates of chosen value persist in single unit firing until the end of the decision epoch.
results.evaluation: Claims C154-C156 appropriately acknowledge limitations and complexities in the interpretation. C156 is supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1. These caveats demonstrate appropriate scientific caution and identify areas for future investigation.

results.result: The analysis does not test the possibility that a third unobserved variable could jointly affect both regions differentially on effort vs. delay trials.
results.evaluation: Claim C164 appropriately acknowledges a limitation in the causal interpretation of the inter-regional interaction findings. This is an important caveat for claims C51-C52 and C162, though it does not invalidate the descriptive findings about task-specific interactions.

results.result: The findings suggest directions for future research, including linking LFP latency measures to spike-LFP coupling and inter-regional coherence, developing hierarchical network models, and testing predictions about distributed competition across reference frames.
results.evaluation: Claims C167 and C175-C177 propose future research directions based on the current findings. While these are reasonable suggestions supported by citations, they represent speculation about future work rather than current results. The proposals are appropriately framed as suggestions rather than conclusions.

results.result: The network model captures dynamics of a single cortical region but not interactions between regions. Competitive dynamics were visible in DLPFC but not other regions at the single-unit level, while mesoscopic dynamics were similar across regions. The authors propose that competition may proceed in a distributed fashion across multiple areas in different reference frames.
results.evaluation: Claims C168-C174 discuss limitations of the single-region network model and propose a distributed account of decision-making. The observations about regional differences (C169-C170) are supported by Figures 1B, 1—figure supplement 1, and 2E. The distributed account (C171-C172) is appropriately presented as a theoretical proposal rather than a demonstrated result.

results.result: PCA was selected for its simplicity and known properties of returning temporal derivatives for variable-duration responses. The approach automatically identifies orthogonal variation in early sensory and late decision-related components, leverages high signal-to-noise mesoscopic dynamics, and does not require first relating activity to experimental variables.
results.evaluation: Claims C178-C189 discuss methodological considerations and advantages of the PCA approach. The observations about orthogonal components (C182-C184) are supported by comparing Figures 1D and 2B. The comparison to motor cortex studies (C185) and advantages over spike-based approaches (C187-C189) are appropriately supported by citations and logical arguments.
